notes.core: A static factory is a named class-level creation operation. It can make intent clear, reuse immutable instances and hide implementation types; it is not automatically a Factory Method design-pattern implementation.
nuance: Do not teach that every factory caches or is faster.
Do not conflate a static factory with a design-pattern factory or a dependency-injection container.
A factory can complement a constructor; neither is universally superior.
rules: Choose a descriptive factory when multiple same-typed creation modes would be ambiguous as constructors.
Factories may return reused objects or private implementation subtypes, but their APIs must specify identity or freshness when callers depend on it.
Returning only through inaccessible constructors can foreclose ordinary subclassing; discoverability and documentation matter.
Factory naming conventions express intent, but implementation can change while honoring contract.

notes.core: Builders address many optional or same-typed parameters; validate single-value constraints at setting time and cross-field invariants on the snapshot used to create the final object.
nuance: A builder for two simple parameters adds needless boilerplate.
Do not expose a builder live collection by reference into the final value.
The book illustrates builder hierarchies, but hierarchy complexity can itself be a reason to simplify the design.
rules: Telescoping constructors can be unreadable when many optional parameters share primitive types.
Mutable JavaBeans configuration can expose invalid intermediate states and require synchronization.
Check cross-field invariants against values copied into the produced object, not earlier mutable builder state.
Builders support fluent immutable construction and hierarchical variants, at some complexity and allocation cost.

notes.core: try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources predictably, on success and failure, preserving the main failure and recording close failures as suppressed exceptions.
nuance: try-with-resources is not a transaction commit guarantee.
A resource requires AutoCloseable (or compatible semantics), not merely an arbitrary close-like method.
Failure should never be declared solved merely by closing without checking data correctness.
rules: Resources in the try declaration close automatically in reverse declaration order.
When the body and close both throw, the body failure remains primary and a close failure is suppressed.
If no body failure occurs and closing fails, a close failure can be the primary failure.
Close failures should be logged or surfaced according to API policy; silent swallowing conceals incomplete work.

notes.core: Value equality is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent while relevant state is unchanged, and false for null. Implementation must correctly override equals(Object).
nuance: Equality across subclass boundaries is a domain choice requiring careful invariants; no universal instanceof/getClass answer without considering hierarchy.
Mutable fields in equality are a dangerous choice for object stability and hashed collections.
Hashing compatibility is specified separately by Item 11.
rules: When superclass identity equality is already appropriate, do not override by reflex.
An equality definition on subclasses with added value fields can break symmetry or transitivity; prefer composition to mix extra information with a base value.
Never overload equals(T) in place of overriding equals(Object); use @Override to catch signatures.
Test positive, negative, reverse-order and triple relationships; avoid comparing unrelated types as equal.

notes.trap: One-sided cross-type equality makes a.equals(b) different from b.equals(a).

notes.core: Whenever equals gives value semantics, hashCode must assign equal values the same int. Hash collisions are legal; good distribution primarily matters for performance.
nuance: Never assert equal hash codes imply equal objects.
A record typically derives equals and hashCode from components; component mutability may still create map-key hazards.
Do not micro-optimize hashCode without profiling.
rules: A HashMap lookup by a logically equal fresh key depends on matching hash codes.
Unequal objects may share a hash code: hashing is not an equality proof.
Relevant equality fields should inform hashing; omitting meaningful variation can cause excessive collisions.
Caching hash codes is safest for effectively immutable values; Objects.hash is convenient but may allocate and box.

notes.title: Equal values must hash alike
notes.trap: Overriding equals for a key but inheriting Object.hashCode, leading to missing retrievals.

notes.core: An immutable value preserves observable state after creation: control subclassing, restrict mutators, guard mutable components, use correct field lifetime, and expose functional updates instead of mutation.
nuance: Some immutable types can cache derived values in carefully controlled nonfinal fields.
Immutable repeated intermediate allocations can cost time/space: design batch operations or a mutable private companion when justified.
Immutable object identity versus value equality is a distinct concern.
rules: No exposed mutator may change observable state after creation.
Prevent subclasses from injecting mutable behavior or otherwise weakening the immutable contract.
Prefer private final fields for core state and exclusive control over all referenced mutable members.
Defensively copy mutable inputs and outputs; ordinary final fields protect references, not their transitive graphs.

notes.core: Subclass reuse across implementation boundaries is fragile when superclass behavior or self-calls change. Prefer composition and delegation when the wrapper is not a genuine subtype or needs independent behavior.
nuance: Composition is not always better; an actual subtype with a supported extension contract can justify inheritance.
Forwarding does not automatically preserve equals, hashCode and identity expectations.
Be careful what an instrumentation count means: calls, attempts, or actual successful additions.
rules: Subclassing is appropriate for a true is-a relationship with a superclass designed and documented for extension.
Overriding one mutator may be re-entered by inherited bulk mutators, invalidating instrumentation or checks.
A wrapper around an interface isolates internal implementation details but requires correct forwarding of all API behavior.
Wrapper callbacks may bypass the wrapper because the wrapped object can register itself (self-reference caveat).

notes.core: Copy mutable caller-supplied data into owned representations before validating dependent invariants; also avoid exposing internal mutable references through accessors.
nuance: A shallow copy does not protect against mutation of nested elements.
Unmodifiable view of an externally owned mutable collection is not an immutable snapshot.
This prevents alias-based invariant violations; it does not prove all concurrency races impossible without further synchronization.
rules: If a constructor stores mutable inputs, it must ordinarily take ownership by copying before validation, protecting against concurrent mutations during the validation window.
If a getter hands out an internal mutable object, callers can modify the owner’s state unless the value is copied or wrapped safely.
For subclassable input types, calling their clone() is not a general security boundary.
Document intentional ownership-transfer APIs explicitly, and consider performance only when justified by trust and measurement.
